Day 41 of 100 · Linux Administration

Linux Filesystem

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityLinux AdministrationPublished journey entry

The Linux phase began with the filesystem layout: where configuration, logs, variable data, devices and user data live and why location communicates purpose.

Architecture / mental model

/ → /etc configuration · /var changing service data/logs · /home users · /usr programs/data · /tmp temporary · /dev devices · /proc,/sys kernel views

How it works

Linux does not organize the filesystem as a collection of drive letters. A single directory tree gives files a location based on role and mount point.

Knowing the conventional purpose of `/etc`, `/var`, `/home`, `/usr`, `/tmp`, `/dev`, `/proc` and `/sys` makes administration safer because you can predict where a service stores configuration, mutable data and runtime information.

Mount points can place different filesystems under the same tree, so a path that looks nearby can live on a completely different device or storage backend.

Hands-on reference

pwd
ls -lah /
findmnt
df -hT

Verification

Use `findmnt` and `df -hT` to map important paths to their real filesystems, then inspect the service directories you plan to automate before editing anything.

Field note / gotcha

Path proximity does not mean storage proximity. `/var` may be a separate filesystem even though it appears directly under `/`.

Security considerations

Permissions, mount options and ownership all depend on where data lives. Sensitive configuration and writable application data should not be treated as interchangeable.

What I learned

Filesystem literacy turns 'where did Linux put it?' into a question you can usually answer from convention and mounts.
